title: Saskatoon police to keep Tasers
article: Saskatoon city police say they will continue deploying Taser stun guns despite recent deaths related to their use in Canada, but the police force's plans to order more Tasers are open to review.
Police in Vancouver announced Friday that a man, high on cocaine and other drugs, died after a police Taser shock -- the fifth such confirmed death in Canada.
"Until such time that somebody, probably the government, suggests that Tasers are not suitable for police use then we are going to continue to use Tasers," said Saskatoon police Insp. Al Stickney.
Two Tasers are stored by the police's emergency response team, but neither have ever been used except in training, said Stickney.

Tasers fire two tiny hooks that stick in the target's skin and conduct 50,000 volts of electricity into the victim through tiny wires. The current lasts for seconds and renders muscles unusable for minutes -- ideally leaving no permanent injury.
Last year the city allocated $62,000 to buy 34 additional Tasers for patrol cars by 2005, but Stickney said the decision is not final.

"It will be made based on budgetary priorities and it will probably depend somewhat on things like the issue in Vancouver and whether they're, at the end of the day, deemed safe for police usage," said Stickney.
Saskatoon police looked into Tasers as a non-lethal alternative after officers shot and killed Keldon McMillan in 2001 after he threatened to shoot at officers following a chase.
Amnesty International said the weapons should be banned until further testing has been done or strict regulations are made as to which individuals should be targeted.
The organization says the weapon has only been tested on those in good health, and victims with underlying health problems can potentially be killed.
But Tasers can provide a safer alternative to other measures, said Stickney.
"It's in there as one of the use-of-force options, and that is based on an individual officer's response to a situation," said Stickney. "We can't pin down exactly when a Taser would be appropriate."

Deb McEwen, spokesperson for the Saskatchewan Police Commission, the regulatory body responsible for municipal police services, says Tasers are available for use by officers in emergency situations only under orders from the chief.
